extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, argumentation theorists, and mathematicians interested in the nature of proof, explanation, and argument
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and evaluate distinctions and connections between mathematical proof, argument, and explanation; identify criteria that make a proof explanatory versus merely justificatory. The page is a scholarly discussion surveying competing theoretical criteria and their limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard pragmatic criterion (argument vs explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument’s purpose is to get the hearer to accept something doubtful; an explanation’s purpose is to get the hearer to understand something already accepted as a fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used (Hamblin, Walton, contemporary dialectical theories). The paper emphasizes limitations in mathematics: a theorem cannot be considered 'already accepted' independently of proofs, so pragmatic distinction may be insufficient. The author notes this criterion is useful in familiar dialogical situations but fails when agents' epistemic positions are unknown or when proofs are long and reveal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural (causal) criterion for explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations at the propositional level employ causal relations, whereas argumentation has no such restriction (Snoeck Henkemans’ claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper points out limits: not all explanations are causal, and causality is problematic in pure mathematics, so a causality-based restriction will not generally work for mathematical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined pragmatic+structural account / 'tough cases' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages can be both argumentative and explanatory when pragmatic and structural features coincide or balance (Govier’s observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain instances where statements justify (in contexts of doubt) and explain (by specifying underlying structures). In mathematics, 'underlying structures' might play the explanatory role when causal notions are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical-tier requirement for being an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument requires not only an illative (logical) core but also a dialectical tier: manifest open‑mindedness and attention to objections, misguided or irrelevant criticisms (Johnson’s view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: many mathematical proofs lack an explicit dialectical tier and so, on this account, would not qualify as arguments. The author critiques over-contextualization of this notion but acknowledges the importance of pragmatic dimension in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman’s rhetorical plausibility boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Argumentation is the proper field of what is likely, plausible, or probable; proofs (certainties of calculation) lie outside the domain of argument (Perelman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a sharp boundary excluding rigorous mathematical proof from argumentation theory; author notes the boundary is historically and practically fuzzy and that trading zones exist where mathematical argumentation occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hempel’s DN (deductive-nomological) pragmatic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation and argument are both answers to why-questions; the difference is the status of the conclusion (is it dubious or not?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hempel's account is monological (impersonal 'we' or 'Science'), which the author calls 'half-pragmatic'. In mathematics, because a theorem's acceptance depends on proof, Hempel’s pragmatic distinction runs into problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Fraassen’s contrast-class (context-dependent why-question) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation is an answer to 'Why p?' relative to a contrast class determined by context and the questioner’s interests; explanatory proofs provide the right kind of information expected by that why-question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resnik & Kushner adopt this to say explanatory proofs supply information the questioner seeks. The author notes Sandborg’s objections: probability-based grading and the limits of contrast classes in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner’s characterizing-property criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain the behavior of an entity is to deduce it from the entity's essence or nature; explanatory proofs deduce from a 'characterizing property' unique within a domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner’s account connects explanation to deducing behavior from essential properties or unique characterizing features. It downplays pragmatics and emphasizes that explanatory proofs are those that make conclusions easier to understand by showing their grounding in an entity’s nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic-account / independence criterion (Resnik & Kushner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs explain only if they give a systematic account; if explaining requires systematic accounting, almost any proof could count, but Resnik & Kushner are skeptical that proofs typically explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They argue mathematicians 'rarely describe themselves as explaining' and doubt there is a clear criterion to identify explanatory proofs; the author recounts this skepticism and contrasts it with historical mathematicians' preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-circularity requirement for explanatory induction (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one mathematical truth helps explain another, the explanatory relation must be non-circular: the explanans must not in turn be partly explained by the explanandum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that inductive proofs are generally not explanatory; the author notes this principle is open to discussion and contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-appeal / apparent adequacy criterion (Polya)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must not only be correct but must 'appear' adequate to the reader; explanatory proofs avoid puzzling 'deus ex machina' introductions of auxiliary entities and provide an overview or strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya’s examples show that proofs that are puzzling to readers (even if correct) fail to explain; he offers alternative proofs as strategic enhancements to dissolve puzzlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace vs deep explanation distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace explanation: the sequence of inferences leading to the conclusion (may not enlighten non-experts). Deep explanation: appeals to the addressee’s knowledge base and gives insight into the 'idea' behind the proof (Walton/Polya/Weyl terminology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishing these helps explain why some proofs feel explanatory even if logically equivalent to non-explanatory ones; deep explanations provide architects' overview vs masons' link-by-link deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandborg’s accessibility/contrast-class expansion critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs may provide conceptual resources beyond the contrast class presumed by the questioner; grading explanations by probability (Van Fraassen style) is inadequate in mathematics where proofs are not probabilistically graded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sandborg uses Polya’s example: a second proof may go conceptually further than the questioner’s presuppositions and so be more explanatory despite not answering the original why-question narrowly construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and community-relative nature of explanatory status
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory status may be a matter of degree and relative to a community’s preferences about structure, ontology, and acceptable patterns of explanation; not purely subjective but community- or field-relative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues most explanatory proofs should be telling to most people in a community; explanatory stores (Kitcher) and tastes change over time and across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher’s unification / pattern-of-argument criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain is to fit phenomena into a unified picture via a pattern of argument instantiated with non-logical terms; explanatory virtue arises from unification and the availability of acceptable argument patterns to a community (explanatory store over K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher’s model emphasizes structural unification, gives a normative theory linking explanation and understanding, and makes explanatory acceptability relative to a group’s beliefs K. The paper notes Kitcher is mostly structural and 'half-pragmatic' because it leaves vague whose understanding counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding-as-integration criterion (architecture/simplification/unification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs provide understanding by integrating results within a favored frame of intelligibility via architecture, organization, simplification, systematization, or unification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with Peirce, Weyl, Kitcher. The author emphasizes that understanding is psychologically tinged, sometimes illusory, and that explanatory value often depends on cognitive satisfaction (overview, roadmap) as much as on formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-readiness / pattern-acceptance criterion (Newton example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof or unifying argument counts as explanatory depends on whether the audience is ready to accept the particular pattern or 'filling instructions' used to instantiate the argument pattern as explanatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Newton’s mathematical unification was acceptable mathematically but not acceptable as a physical explanation to French contemporaries who rejected his hypotheses. The paper stresses audience and field sensitivities.
